walkthroughs.body_html:
If you do not put the first item back, the totals shrink. The second probability is conditional on the first.

Example: 5 red and 3 blue counters (8 total).

  • P(red 1st) = 5/8
  • If red was drawn, now 4 red and 3 blue remain (7 total). P(red 2nd | red 1st) = 4/7

P(red, red) = 5/8 × 4/7 = 20/56 = 5/14

If you repeat an experiment many times, how often do you expect an event?

Expected frequency = P(event) × number of trials

Example: a fair dice rolled 60 times. P(rolling a 6) = 1/6.

Expected number of 6s = 1/6 × 60 = 10.

This is an estimate — actual results will vary.

Every event A has a complement: "not A". Together they cover every possibility.

P(not A) = 1 − P(A)

This is brilliant for "at least one" questions. P(at least one six in two rolls) = 1 − P(no sixes) = 1 − (5/6 × 5/6) = 1 − 25/36 = 11/36.

mcqs.q: When picking WITHOUT replacement, what changes for the second pick?
options: Nothing — probabilities stay the same
The totals shrink, so probabilities change
Only the favourable outcomes change
The events become mutually exclusive

mcqs.q: If P(A) = 0.8, what is P(not A)?
If you've flipped a fair coin and got heads 5 times in a row, what is the probability the next flip is heads?
options: 1/2 — each flip is independent of the previous ones.
1 because the coin has clearly been biased by the previous flips.
Less than 1/2, because the coin is 'due' to land on tails to balance the results.
Yes, but only when the probabilities are equal.

mcqs.q: Are 'independent events' and 'mutually exclusive events' the same?
options: No — independent events do not affect each other's probability; mutually exclusive events cannot both happen.
Yes, but only when the probabilities are equal.
Yes — both mean the events are unrelated.
Yes, but only when expressed as a percentage.

mcqs.q: Can a probability ever be greater than 1?
options: No — probabilities range from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).
Yes — if an event is very likely, the probability can be 1.5 or 2.
Yes, but only when expressed as a percentage.
1 because the coin has clearly been biased by the previous flips.
